en.title: The quiet hour before the city wakes
en.excerpt: Why I started getting up at five — not for productivity, but for the particular silence that belongs to no one. On coffee, cold air and doing absolutely nothing well.
en.content:
It started as insomnia and became a religion. At five in the morning the city hasn't decided what it is yet — the bakery ovens are on but the shutters are down, and the light belongs to nobody in particular.

I want to be clear about something: this is not a productivity essay. I do not journal, ice-bathe or optimize at five a.m. Mostly I sit near the window with coffee and watch the streetlamp switch itself off, which it does at 5:42 with an air of quiet professionalism.

The hour has rules, though I never wrote them down until now:

  • No phone. The phone stays in the hallway, sulking.
  • One coffee, made the long way.
  • Nothing that could be called a task.
The point of the quiet hour is that it produces nothing. That's the whole product.

My grandmother used to call this sitting with the house. She'd be up before everyone, not doing anything you could name, and if you came downstairs early she'd look mildly betrayed. I understand her completely now.

What the silence is actually like

People imagine early-morning silence as an absence. It isn't — it's a different set of sounds with the volume rebalanced. The refrigerator has opinions. A neighbour's pipes clear their throat. Around 5:30 the first blackbird files its report.

By six, the spell thins. Cars. A door. Someone's alarm through the wall, snoozed twice. The city remembers itself, and I hand the morning back.

If you want to try it

Don't set out to wake at five; set out to be unavailable for one hour. The hour can be anywhere. Early just makes it easier — no one expects you, so no one interrupts. Start with twenty minutes. Make the coffee the long way. Let the streetlamp do its thing.

That's all. Nothing was achieved this morning, and I recommend it completely.
en.author: June Marsk
